Lecture 27

Laplace inversion by complex integration

We prove the uniqueness of the Laplace transform and derive the Bromwich inversion formula from Fourier inversion, with its limit and its values at jumps. We evaluate the inversion integral by closing the contour around poles and around a branch cut, and we check each inverse by its causal support, its initial and late behaviour and its forward transform.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • State the uniqueness theorem of the Laplace transform and use it to identify a signal, including impulses.
  • State the Bromwich formula with its symmetric limit and its values at jumps and at t=0t=0t=0, and derive it from Fourier inversion.
  • Invert a transform by residues, checking the growth of FFF on the added arcs separately from Jordan’s estimate.
  • Check an inverse by its causal support, its initial value, its behaviour for large ttt and its forward transform.

Lecture 26 computed Laplace transforms only in the forward direction, from a signal to its transform. Solving an initial-value problem by transforms needs the opposite step: the algebra produces a transform FFF, and we want the signal fff. This lecture first proves that a transform determines its signal, so that a table may be read from right to left. It then recovers the signal by an integral of estF(s)\ee^{st}F(s)estF(s) along a vertical line, which comes from the Fourier inversion theorems of Lecture 23. Finally it evaluates that integral by the residues and contours of Lectures 19 and 20. The lecture reads in three stages: uniqueness and the inversion integral (Sections 27.1 and 27.2), closing the contour (Sections 27.3–27.5), and checks on an inverse with a branch cut that leads to the diffusion kernel (Sections 27.6 and 27.7).

27.1 Uniqueness of the transform

We use the class of Lecture 26. A function fff on (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞) is piecewise continuous if on every bounded subinterval of (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), including intervals (0,β](0,\beta](0,β], it is continuous except at finitely many points, with finite one-sided limits there. So its exceptional points do not accumulate at 000, although fff itself may be unbounded near 000. It is transformable at a real number ccc if ∫0∞e−ct∣f(t)∣ ⁣dt<∞\int_0^\infty\ee^{-ct}\abs{f(t)}\dd t<\infty∫0∞​e−ct∣f(t)∣dt<∞, and cfc_fcf​ is its abscissa of absolute convergence. Its transform F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t) ⁣dtF(s)=\int_0^\infty\ee^{-st}f(t)\dd tF(s)=∫0∞​e−stf(t)dt is analytic on the half-plane Re⁡s>cf\Re s>c_fRes>cf​ (Lecture 26).

27.2 The Bromwich integral

On a vertical line in its half-plane the Laplace transform is a Fourier transform (Lecture 26). Lecture 23 inverted Fourier transforms, so we obtain an inversion formula for Laplace transforms. The formula (27.2) is the Bromwich integral, also called the Riemann–Mellin formula. We read it as follows.

  • The limit is symmetric. The same cutoff RRR is used above and below the real axis, as in Lecture 23. For a signal with a jump, the two one-sided improper integrals need not converge separately: for F=1/sF=1/sF=1/s, c>0c>0c>0 and t=0t=0t=0 the segment integral is π−1arctan⁡(R/c)→12\pi^{-1}\arctan(R/c)\to\tfrac12π−1arctan(R/c)→21​, while over [c−iR1,c+iR2][c-\iu R_1,c+\iu R_2][c−iR1​,c+iR2​] its imaginary part −ln⁡((c2+R22)/(c2+R12))/(4π)-\ln\bigl((c^2+R_2^2)/(c^2+R_1^2)\bigr)/(4\pi)−ln((c2+R22​)/(c2+R12​))/(4π) has no limit.

  • Values at jumps. At a jump the formula gives the half-sum of the one-sided limits, not the value of fff, which the transform does not determine. At t=0t=0t=0 it gives 12f(0+)\tfrac12f(0^+)21​f(0+), because the causal signal jumps from 000 to f(0+)f(0^+)f(0+) there, and for t<0t<0t<0 it gives 000.

The impulse δ(t−a)\dirac(t-a)δ(t−a) is identified by Proposition 27.3.

27.3 Closing the contour: poles

In the second stage we evaluate the Bromwich integral by residues. As in Lecture 19, we close the segment by an arc, evaluate the closed integral by residues and show that the arc contributes nothing in the limit. For t>0t>0t>0 the factor est\ee^{st}est is small where Re⁡s\Re sRes is very negative, so we close to the left. For R>0R>0R>0 let ARleftA^{\mathrm{left}}_RARleft​ be the semicircle with centre ccc and radius RRR that runs from c+iRc+\iu Rc+iR through c−Rc-Rc−R to c−iRc-\iu Rc−iR, and let ARrightA^{\mathrm{right}}_RARright​ be the semicircle that runs from c−iRc-\iu Rc−iR through c+Rc+Rc+R to c+iRc+\iu Rc+iR (Figure 27.1). The segment followed by ARleftA^{\mathrm{left}}_RARleft​ is a closed path around the left half-disc. The segment followed by ARrightA^{\mathrm{right}}_RARright​ traversed backwards, from c+iRc+\iu Rc+iR to c−iRc-\iu Rc−iR, is a closed path around the right half-disc.

For rational transforms the residues give the signal directly, by partial fractions and the forward transforms of Lecture 26.

Summary

A Laplace transform determines its signal up to values at finitely many points in each bounded interval, and a signal with impulses including its impulses. On a vertical line Re⁡s=c\Re s=cRes=c the Laplace transform is the Fourier transform of e−ctf(t)\ee^{-ct}f(t)e−ctf(t), so Fourier inversion with symmetric cutoffs gives the Bromwich integral. Closing its segment to the left evaluates it by residues, provided the transform tends to zero on the arcs; Jordan’s estimate handles the factor est\ee^{st}est separately.

  • Uniqueness: F=GF=GF=G on a real ray s>s0s>s_0s>s0​ implies f=gf=gf=g at every t>0t>0t>0 where f−gf-gf−g is continuous; impulses are determined too.

  • Bromwich: for fff piecewise C1C^1C1 on [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞) and transformable at ccc, the limit as R→∞R\to\inftyR→∞ of (2πi)−1∫c−iRc+iRestF ⁣ds(2\pi\iu)^{-1}\int_{c-\iu R}^{c+\iu R}\ee^{st}F\dd s(2πi)−1∫c−iRc+iR​estFds is 12(f(t+)+f(t−))\tfrac12(f(t^+)+f(t^-))21​(f(t+)+f(t−)) for t>0t>0t>0, 12f(0+)\tfrac12f(0^+)21​f(0+) at t=0t=0t=0 and 000 for t<0t<0t<0.

  • Residues: with finitely many singular points left of the line and max⁡ARleft∣F∣→0\max_{A^{\mathrm{left}}_R}\abs F\to0maxARleft​​∣F∣→0, the half-sum equals ∑jRes⁡s=sj(estF)\sum_j\Res_{s=s_j}(\ee^{st}F)∑j​Ress=sj​​(estF) for t>0t>0t>0; for rational FFF the residue sum is the continuous inverse.

  • Closures: e−asG\ee^{-as}Ge−asG: close left for t>at>at>a, right for t<at<at<a; for a periodic signal the residues are its Fourier coefficients; e−xs/D/(2Ds)\ee^{-x\sqrt{s/D}}/(2\sqrt{Ds})e−xs/D​/(2Ds​): a cut along (−∞,0](-\infty,0](−∞,0] gives e−x2/(4Dt)/4πDt\ee^{-x^2/(4Dt)}/\sqrt{4\pi Dt}e−x2/(4Dt)/4πDt​.

  • Checks: support, sF(s)→f(0+)sF(s)\to f(0^+)sF(s)→f(0+) as s→∞s\to\inftys→∞, sF(s)→ℓsF(s)\to\ellsF(s)→ℓ as s→0+s\to0^+s→0+ when f(t)→ℓf(t)\to\ellf(t)→ℓ (not conversely), rightmost singular points, forward transform.

Lecture 28 uses uniqueness, inversion by residues and the transfer function to solve complete physical initial-value problems.

Preparation: Lectures 7 and 9 (uniqueness, the oscillator), 16 (the principal square root on a cut), 17 (roots of polynomials), 18 (Cauchy’s theorem on star-shaped sets, the identity theorem, residues, the Gaussian integral with a complex parameter), 19 (the residue theorem, winding numbers of half-discs, Jordan’s estimate, bounds for a rational function), 20 (splitting a cut contour), 22 (the rules I1–I3), 23 (inversion with symmetric cutoffs), 25 (uniqueness of the Fourier transform), 26 (transformable functions, the bridge, analyticity, integration, delay, impulses, periodic signals); GM 26, 27, 35 (the cited convergence of Fourier series) and 38 (the Gaussian integral).

Reading: M. J. Ablowitz and A. S. Fokas, Introduction to Complex Variables and Applications, §4.5 (the Bromwich contour with arcs s=c+Reiθs=c+R\ee^{\iu\theta}s=c+Reiθ, Examples 4.5.2 and 4.5.3, the latter with a cut along the negative real axis; Exercise 14(c) is the square-root transform of this lecture) and §4.6; Riley, Hobson and Bence, Mathematical Methods for Physics and Engineering, 3rd ed., §25.5 (the Bromwich integral, the contour completions of Figure 25.7 and a delayed pulse).
